analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on investment gains and stock dividends for individuals and corporations.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Jon Kyl with three Senate Republicans behind it, the bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have allowed individual taxpayers to deduct 70% of their capital gains from taxable income and exclude 70% of the dividends they receive from domestic corporations, and would have cut the corporate alternative capital gains tax rate from 35% to 22% [S2][S3]. It contained no offsetting revenue increases [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals with capital gains and stock dividends would gain the most: the bill would let non-corporate taxpayers deduct 70% of their net capital gain from gross income and exclude 70% of dividends from domestic corporations, cutting the top effective tax rate on both to roughly 12% [S2][S3]. Corporations would also gain, with the alternative capital gains tax rate cut from 35% to 22% [S3]. Because investment income is heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, the benefits would flow overwhelmingly to them [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors and large corporate shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Individuals with capital gains would deduct 70% of net capital gains from gross income, cutting the top effective tax rate on a long-term gain from 39.6% to about 11.9%
Individuals receiving stock dividends would exclude 70% of dividends from domestic corporations from taxable income, cutting the top effective rate on dividends to roughly 12%
Corporations would see the alternative capital gains tax rate reduced from 35% to 22%, lowering tax on corporate asset sales

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the federal Treasury would collect less revenue, since the bill contains no offsetting tax increases — the cost would fall on general taxpayers through higher deficits or reduced government services [S3]. Because capital gains and dividends are concentrated among high-income households, the revenue given up would primarily subsidize taxes on wealthier Americans [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so it would add directly to federal deficits — a cost borne by general taxpayers and future generations rather than by the beneficiaries of the cut

The benefits would be sharply concentrated: capital gains and dividend income go overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households, so a broad revenue loss would be exchanged for a narrow tax cut at the top

Reducing taxes on capital gains relative to ordinary wages would widen the gap in how work income and investment income are taxed, increasing incentives to recharacterize labor income as investment income

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits and costs are badly lopsided. A large, unoffset revenue loss would have been spread across all taxpayers through bigger deficits, while the tax relief would concentrate on households with the most capital gains and dividends — roughly a 12% top rate on investment income versus 39.6% on wages. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill finances a cut for investors with general taxpayer money, and that no offsetting savings were proposed. Its quiet death in committee meant the trade-off was never seriously tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without ever getting a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, with Sen. Paul Coverdell as an original cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day
Only two additional senators cosponsored the bill during the entire Congress
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the record — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers are better off than they would have been under the bill, since the unoffset revenue loss never occurred. Wealthy investors gained nothing, but also lost nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; taxpayers avoided the revenue loss

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on its behalf when it was introduced

for.name: Sen. Paul Coverdell
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only visible support was three Republican senators sponsoring it in a Republican-led Senate Finance Committee that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would cut the top effective tax rate on long-term capital gains and domestic dividends to roughly 12% by excluding 70% of both from income. Because most capital gains and dividends go to the highest-income households, the tax cut's value would concentrate at the top while the unoffset revenue loss would be shared by all taxpayers.
The bill would cut the alternative capital gains tax rate for corporations from 35% to 22%, lowering taxes on corporate asset sales and restructuring gains.

The bill includes special coordination rules for regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and other pass-through entities, easing the transition to the lower rates for fund investors. Lower taxes on fund distributions would make fund investing modestly more attractive.
